transcript: Sure, my name is Mary Peltola. I was born and raised in Bethel along the Cusco Coom River, actually three little villages outside of Bethel. I grew up commercial fishing for kings at the beginning of the season, and then chums right after that, and reds, and then we finished up with silvers. And my family also had a tender boat operation. My dad ran a tender boat. And then my sister and I were captains of a commercial fishing boat different times over the years. So that's how I was raised. I worked for Fish and Game when I was in college. I imagined I was going to become a teacher, and so I went to college teacher training. And as it happened, I did a legislative internship at the Capitol in Juneau in 1996, and really was drawn to public policy in the public process. And in 1996, I ran for office, I ran for State House, and I lost by 56 votes. But in 1998, I was elected and then reelected for more time. So I served 10 years in the State House. So that's a little bit about me.

transcript: Well, primarily my interest was on reauthorizing Magnuson Stevens Act. I think everyone recognizes that we are living in a very different paradigm than the one we had before 2010. I would say we don't have the abundance that we're accustomed to as Alaskans. And that's presenting a myriad of food security issues on the West Coast of Alaska. And it's been surprising to me how little that's been talked about and how little action has been taken on that. And it's really been status quo. We've been in this low abundance paradigm for 13 summers now. And we don't see traction in terms of policy or really investing in science. And there seems to be an attitude at the policy level that until we know why these things are happening, we can't do anything.
